questions.question: What are the time complexities of common sorting algorithms?
questions.title: Sorting Algorithm Complexities | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Comparison sorts: **bubble**, **insertion**, **selection** are **O(n^2)**; **merge sort** is **O(n log n)** guaranteed; **quicksort** is **O(n log n)** average but **O(n^2)** worst; **heap sort** is **O(n log n)** guaranteed. Non-comparison sorts like **counting/radix** can hit **O(n+k)**. The comparison-sort lower bound is **O(n log n)**. Java's `Arrays.sort` uses dual-pivot quicksort (primitives) and TimSort (objects).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the standard complexities, including quicksort's worst case and the O(n log n) lower bound
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying quicksort is always O(n log n), or forgetting which sorts are stable / in-place
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note the O(n log n) comparison lower bound and that counting sort beats it by not comparing

sections.title: Sorting Complexities and Tradeoffs
sections.content:
**Comparison-based** sorts decide order by comparing elements, and no such sort can beat **O(n log n)** in the worst case (a proven lower bound). The simple ones - **bubble, insertion, selection** - are **O(n^2)** and fine only for tiny or nearly-sorted inputs. The efficient ones - **merge sort** (O(n log n) guaranteed, stable, O(n) space), **heap sort** (O(n log n), in-place, not stable), and **quicksort** (O(n log n) average, **O(n^2) worst**, in-place) - are the workhorses.

**Non-comparison** sorts like **counting** and **radix** sidestep the lower bound by using keys as indices, reaching **O(n + k)** when the key range `k` is small. Java's `Arrays.sort` uses **dual-pivot quicksort** for primitives and **TimSort** (a merge/insertion hybrid) for objects.

sections.title: Sorting Algorithms Compared
sections.content:
| Algorithm | Best | Average | Worst | Space | Stable |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bubble | O(n) | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | O(1) | Yes |
| Insertion | O(n) | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | O(1) | Yes |
| Selection | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | O(n^2) | O(1) | No |
| Merge | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n) | Yes |
| Quick | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | **O(n^2)** | O(log n) | No |
| Heap | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(n log n) | O(1) | No |
| Counting | O(n+k) | O(n+k) | O(n+k) | O(k) | Yes |

sections.title: What Java Uses
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Quicksort always O(n log n)**: its worst case is **O(n^2)** (bad pivots / sorted input).
- **Merge sort is in-place**: it needs **O(n)** auxiliary space.
- **Ignoring stability**: selection/quick/heap are **not stable**; merge and insertion are.
- **Forgetting non-comparison sorts**: counting/radix beat O(n log n) for small key ranges.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Simple sorts: **O(n^2)**; efficient: **O(n log n)**.
- **Quicksort**: O(n log n) avg, **O(n^2) worst**, in-place.
- **Merge**: O(n log n) guaranteed, **stable**, O(n) space.
- Comparison lower bound is **O(n log n)**; counting/radix beat it (O(n+k)).
- Java: **dual-pivot quicksort** (primitives), **TimSort** (objects).

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I'd group them. The simple comparison sorts, bubble, insertion, and selection, are all O of n squared on average, so they're only practical for tiny inputs or nearly-sorted data, where insertion sort in particular is close to linear. The efficient comparison sorts are O of n log n. Merge sort is O of n log n guaranteed, it's stable, but it needs O of n extra space. Heap sort is also O of n log n guaranteed and it's in place, but it's not stable. Quicksort is the interesting one: it's O of n log n on average and in place, but its worst case is O of n squared, which happens with bad pivot choices, classically on already-sorted input with a naive pivot. A key fact I'd state is that no comparison-based sort can do better than O of n log n in the worst case; that's a proven lower bound, because comparisons can only extract so much information. Non-comparison sorts like counting sort and radix sort get around that by using the values themselves as indices rather than comparing, so they can run in O of n plus k, where k is the range of keys, but they only help when that range is small. Finally, I'd mention what Java actually uses, because it shows practical knowledge: Arrays dot sort uses a dual-pivot quicksort for primitive arrays, and TimSort, which is a hybrid of merge and insertion sort, for object arrays. The reason for the split is stability, primitives don't need it, but objects sorted by a key do.

questions.question: How does bubble sort work and when would you actually use it?
questions.title: Bubble Sort Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Bubble sort** repeatedly walks the array swapping **adjacent out-of-order pairs**, so the largest unsorted element 'bubbles' to the end each pass. It's **O(n^2)** time, **O(1)** space, and **stable**. With an **early-exit flag** (stop when a pass makes no swaps), it becomes **O(n)** on already-sorted data. In practice you'd never use it for real sorting - it's a teaching algorithm.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement it, add the early-exit optimization, and admit it's impractical at scale
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the early-termination flag, or claiming bubble sort is useful for large data
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Add the swapped-flag optimization for O(n) best case and explain it's stable but rarely used

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Swaps **adjacent** pairs; largest bubbles to the end each pass.
- **O(n^2)** time, **O(1)** space, **stable**.
- **swapped flag** -> **O(n)** best case on sorted input.
- Inner loop shrinks by `i` (last `i` are sorted).
- A **teaching** algorithm; not used in production.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Bubble sort works by making repeated passes over the array, and on each pass it compares adjacent pairs of elements and swaps them if they're in the wrong order. The effect is that the largest unsorted element bubbles up to the end of the array in each pass, like a bubble rising to the surface. After the first pass the largest element is in its final spot, after the second pass the two largest are, and so on, which means each subsequent pass can stop a little earlier because the tail is already sorted. The time complexity is O of n squared, because I do roughly n passes and each pass does up to n comparisons. It uses O of one extra space since it sorts in place, and it's stable, meaning equal elements keep their relative order. The one optimization actually worth adding is a swapped flag. At the start of each pass I set it to false, and I set it true whenever I make a swap. If I finish a full pass without any swaps, the array must already be sorted, so I break out early. That makes the best case O of n on already-sorted input. I'd be honest in an interview that bubble sort is a teaching algorithm. It's intuitive and easy to reason about, which is why it's taught first, but because it's quadratic you'd never use it for real data; you'd reach for Arrays dot sort or merge or quicksort. So I can implement it cleanly with the optimization, but I also know when not to use it.

sections.title: Adjacent inversions and the early-exit flag
sections.content:
Bubble sort repeatedly compares neighboring values and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. After one complete pass, the largest value in the unsorted part has moved to its final position at the right.

**Worked example: `[5, 1, 4, 2]`**

The first pass swaps 5 with 1, then 5 with 4, then 5 with 2, producing `[1, 4, 2, 5]`. The last position is now fixed. The next pass keeps 1, swaps 4 with 2, and produces `[1, 2, 4, 5]`. A further pass makes no swaps, so the early-exit flag proves the array is sorted.

After pass `p`, the last `p` elements never need to be compared again. Reducing the inner loop by the pass number avoids useless work. Swapping only when `left > right`, not when values are equal, makes the algorithm stable.

The average and worst cases are O(n²), with O(1) extra space. With an early-exit flag, an already sorted array takes O(n). Bubble sort is useful for learning swaps and loop invariants or for tiny teaching examples, but Java library sorting or insertion sort is normally a better practical choice.

sections.title: Bubble Sort Passes
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[for each pass] --> B[swapped = false]
    B --> C[compare adjacent pairs]
    C --> D{a j > a j+1?}
    D -- yes --> E[swap, swapped = true]
    D -- no --> F[next pair]
    E --> F
    F --> G{end of pass?}
    G -- no --> C
    G -- yes --> H{swapped == false?}
    H -- yes --> Z[done early - sorted]
    H -- no --> A
```

sections.title: Bubble Sort with Early Exit (Dry Run)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **No early-exit flag**: without it, even a sorted array costs O(n^2).
- **Inner bound `j < n-1` always**: use `n-1-i` so settled elements aren't rechecked.
- **Calling it useful at scale**: it's O(n^2) - never for large data.
- **Off-by-one in swaps**: compare `a[j]` with `a[j+1]`, not `a[j-1]`.

sections.title: Where bubble sort fits
sections.content: Bubble sort is easy to trace and can stop in O(n) on an already sorted array, but its O(n²) average work makes it a poor default. Insertion sort is usually better for small or nearly sorted data because it shifts values into a sorted prefix with less repeated swapping. For normal application code, use the Java library sort; choose bubble sort mainly when the exercise is specifically testing its mechanics.

questions.question: What sorting algorithm does Java use internally in Arrays.sort()?
questions.title: Java Arrays.sort Internals | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: `Arrays.sort` uses **two different algorithms**: a **dual-pivot quicksort** for **primitive** arrays (`int[]`, `double[]`, ...) and **TimSort** - a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort - for **object** arrays and `Collections.sort`. The split exists because objects need a **stable** sort and primitives don't (equal primitives are indistinguishable), and TimSort exploits already-ordered 'runs' in real-world data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the primitive-vs-object split and why stability drives it
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying Java uses 'merge sort' or 'quicksort' for everything, missing the dual approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that primitives skip stability (so quicksort is fine) while objects use stable TimSort

sections.title: Two Sorts Inside Arrays.sort
sections.content:
Java's `Arrays.sort` isn't one algorithm. For **primitive** arrays it uses a **dual-pivot quicksort** (Vladimir Yaroslavskiy's variant) - fast, in-place, cache-friendly. For **object** arrays (and `Collections.sort` / `List.sort`) it uses **TimSort**, a hybrid of **merge sort** and **insertion sort** designed by Tim Peters.

The reason for the split is **stability**. Sorting objects by a key often must preserve the relative order of equal elements (stable), and TimSort is stable; quicksort is not. Primitives don't need stability - two equal `int`s are truly identical, so order among them is meaningless - which lets Java use the faster quicksort. TimSort also detects already-sorted **runs**, making it close to **O(n)** on partially ordered real-world data.

sections.title: Primitive vs Object Sorting
sections.content:
blue|Primitives|~int double etc|dual-pivot quicksort|in-place, fast|stability not needed
emerald|Objects|~Integer, String, POJO|TimSort hybrid|merge + insertion|stable, run-aware
amber|Why stable|~equal keys keep order|matters for objects|two equal ints identical|primitives skip it
rose|TimSort edge|~real-world data|detects sorted runs|near O(n) if ordered|guaranteed O(n log n)

sections.title: Seeing the Split
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Java uses merge sort'**: only for objects (TimSort); primitives use quicksort.
- **'Java uses quicksort'**: only for primitives; objects use stable TimSort.
- **Assuming primitive sort is stable**: it's not, but it doesn't matter for primitives.
- **Ignoring TimSort's run detection**: it's near-linear on partially sorted data.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Current OpenJDK implementations use **Dual-Pivot Quicksort** for many primitive-array overloads.
- Object-array sorting uses a **stable TimSort-family** implementation.
- The public object-sort contract promises **stability**; exact internal algorithms are implementation details and may change by JDK.
- Equal primitive values carry no separate object identity whose order needs preserving.
- TimSort takes advantage of existing ordered runs in partially sorted data.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The thing most people get wrong is assuming Arrays dot sort uses a single algorithm. It actually uses two, depending on what you're sorting. For primitive arrays, like int arrays or double arrays, it uses a dual-pivot quicksort. For object arrays, and also for Collections dot sort and List dot sort, it uses TimSort, which is a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort. The reason for that split is stability. A stable sort keeps equal elements in their original relative order, and that matters a lot when you sort objects by a key, for example sorting employees by department while keeping the original ordering within each department. TimSort is stable, so it's the right choice for objects. Quicksort is not stable, but for primitives that's completely fine, because two equal integers are genuinely identical, there's no hidden information to preserve, so order among equal primitives is meaningless. That lets Java use the faster, in-place quicksort for primitives without any downside. The other nice property of TimSort is that it detects already-sorted runs in the data and merges them, so on real-world data that's partially ordered it runs close to linear time, while still guaranteeing O of n log n in the worst case. So my one-line summary is: dual-pivot quicksort for primitives because stability isn't needed, and stable, run-aware TimSort for objects because it usually is.

questions.question: How does insertion sort work and when is it better than O(n log n) sorts?
questions.title: Insertion Sort Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Insertion sort** builds the sorted part one element at a time: take the next element and **shift larger elements right** until it slots into place. It's **O(n^2)** worst case but **O(n)** on **nearly-sorted** data, **O(1)** space, and **stable**. That near-sorted speed and low overhead make it the go-to for **small arrays** - which is exactly why TimSort and quicksort switch to it for small subarrays.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know insertion sort's O(n) near-sorted case and why it's used for small subarrays
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating it as just another O(n^2) sort with no advantages over bubble/selection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain its adaptive O(n) best case and that real libraries fall back to it for small inputs

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Builds a sorted prefix; **shifts** larger elements right to insert.
- **O(n^2)** worst, **O(n)** best (nearly sorted) - **adaptive**.
- **Stable**, **O(1)** space.
- Used by **TimSort/quicksort** for **small subarrays**.
- Beats O(n log n) sorts when n is small or data is nearly sorted.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Insertion sort works the way you'd sort a hand of playing cards. You keep the front of the array as a sorted region, and you grow it one element at a time. You take the next element, call it the key, and you compare it leftward through the sorted region, shifting every element that's larger than the key one position to the right to open up a gap, and then you drop the key into that gap. Its worst case is O of n squared, which happens on reverse-sorted input where every key has to travel all the way to the front. But the reason insertion sort is special, and better than bubble or selection sort in practice, is that it's adaptive. On data that's already sorted or nearly sorted, each key barely has to move, so the inner shifting loop almost never runs, and the whole thing becomes O of n, linear. It's also stable and uses constant extra space. The fact I'd really highlight is that it's not just academic: real production sorts use it. TimSort and dual-pivot quicksort both switch to insertion sort once a subarray gets small, typically under around thirty to fifty elements, because for small or nearly-sorted inputs its low overhead and adaptive behavior actually beat the fancier O of n log n algorithms. So when is it better than an n log n sort? When n is small, or when the data is already close to sorted. That's the answer that shows I understand why it matters beyond the textbook. For example, with `[3, 1, 2]`, insert key `1` by shifting `3` right to get `[1, 3, 2]`. Then insert key `2` by shifting `3` once, producing `[1, 2, 3]`.

sections.title: Growing a sorted prefix
sections.content:
Insertion sort treats the left side of the array as sorted. It removes the next value as the `key`, shifts larger values one position to the right, and inserts the key into the gap.

**Worked example: `[3, 1, 2]`**

The prefix `[3]` is already sorted. For key 1, shift 3 right and place 1 at index 0, producing `[1, 3, 2]`. For key 2, shift 3 once and place 2 between 1 and 3. The final array is `[1, 2, 3]`.

The useful invariant is that indexes before `i` are sorted at the start of every outer-loop round. Values are shifted rather than repeatedly swapped, which keeps the inner operation simple. Using `>` instead of `>=` preserves the order of equal items, so insertion sort is stable.

Worst-case time is O(n²), but an already sorted array needs one comparison per item and takes O(n). Its work is closely related to the number of inversions, so it performs well on small or nearly sorted inputs. It uses O(1) extra space and has low overhead. That is why insertion sort is often used for small runs inside hybrid library algorithms even though its asymptotic worst case is quadratic.

sections.title: Insertion Sort Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[i = 1] --> B{i < n?} B -- no --> Z[sorted] B -- yes --> C[key = a i
j = i - 1] C --> D{j >= 0 AND a j > key?} D -- yes --> E[a j+1 = a j
j--] E --> D D -- no --> F[a j+1 = key
i++] F --> B ```

sections.title: Insertion Sort with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Just another O(n^2)'**: it's **adaptive** - O(n) on nearly-sorted data, unlike selection sort.
- **Shifting wrong direction**: shift larger elements **right**, then insert.
- **Starting at i=0**: the first element is the initial sorted region; start `i` at 1.
- **Underrating it**: real libraries use it for small subarrays for a reason.

sections.title: Adaptive speed versus quadratic worst case
sections.content: Insertion sort uses O(1) extra space, is stable, and can approach O(n) when the input is already or nearly sorted. Its weakness is O(n²) shifts for reverse-ordered or large random input. Merge sort gives predictable O(n log n) but needs an array buffer, while quicksort-style library implementations handle larger primitive arrays more efficiently. Insertion sort is strongest for small ranges and short, mostly ordered runs.

questions.question: Why is merge sort preferred over quicksort for sorting linked lists?
questions.title: Merge Sort vs Quicksort Linked List
questions.direct_answer: **Merge sort** is usually preferred for a linked list because it splits with slow/fast pointers and merges by relinking nodes. It guarantees **O(n log n)** and is stable. Its recursive form uses O(log n) stack space; a bottom-up form can use O(1) auxiliary space. Quicksort can be implemented on a linked list, but partitioning and pivot/tail handling are less natural, it loses array cache locality, and a poor pivot can still cause O(n²) time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you connect merge sort's sequential-access nature to linked-list strengths and quicksort's random-access need to its weakness
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying 'merge sort is just faster' without the random-access argument
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that arrays favor quicksort (cache locality) but linked lists favor merge sort (no random access needed)

sections.title: Why merge sort fits linked lists
sections.content:
A linked list supports fast sequential traversal but no constant-time jump to index `i`. Merge sort fits that shape: find the middle with slow and fast pointers, sort both halves, and merge them by changing `next` links. No elements need to shift and no O(n) array merge buffer is required.

For example, `4 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2` splits into `4 -> 1` and `3 -> 2`. Those halves become `1 -> 4` and `2 -> 3`, then a sequential merge relinks them as `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4`.

Quicksort does **not** strictly require random access; a linked-list partition is possible. It is nevertheless a less natural fit because pivot selection, partition boundaries, and tail management require pointer walks, and the structure loses the cache-friendly indexed partition used on arrays. Quicksort is also usually unstable and can take O(n²) after poor pivot choices.

Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) time. Recursive linked-list merge sort uses O(log n) call-stack space; an iterative bottom-up version can use O(1) auxiliary space. That precise space distinction is better than simply calling every linked-list merge sort “in place.”

sections.title: Merge sort and quicksort on a linked list
sections.content:
emerald|Merge sort|~natural list fit|split with slow and fast|merge by relinking|stable O(n log n)
blue|Quicksort|~possible but awkward|pointer-based partition|poor cache locality|O(n²) bad pivots
amber|Space detail|~depends on form|recursive stack O(log n)|bottom-up auxiliary O(1)|no O(n) merge array
rose|Array contrast|~different memory shape|indexed partition is natural|good cache locality|quicksort often fits arrays

sections.title: Why linked-list quicksort is less natural
Merge sort on a list - pointer splicing
Choose by data structure and requirements
sections.content:
- **Linked list:** merge sort is the usual choice for stable, guaranteed O(n log n) sorting with pointer-based merging.
- **Array of primitives:** a quicksort-style implementation often benefits from indexed access, in-place partitioning, and cache locality.
- **Strict auxiliary-space requirement:** bottom-up list merge sort avoids recursive stack growth; recursive merge sort uses O(log n) stack space.
- **Stability required:** merge sort preserves equal-key order when the merge chooses the left node first.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Merge sort needs only **sequential traversal** and merges by changing links.
- Linked-list merge sort guarantees **O(n log n)** and can be **stable**.
- Recursive form uses **O(log n) stack**; bottom-up form can use **O(1) auxiliary space**.
- Quicksort **can** work on lists, but partition and boundary handling are less natural.
- Arrays often favor quicksort-style partitioning because indexed access and cache locality are available.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Merge sort is normally preferred for a linked list because every step matches what a list does well. I can find the middle with slow and fast pointers, recursively sort the two halves, and merge them by relinking nodes in increasing order. For example, `4 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2` becomes `1 -> 4` and `2 -> 3`, and the merge only changes `next` pointers to produce `1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4`. That gives guaranteed O(n log n) time and can preserve the order of equal keys. I would be precise about space: the common recursive version uses O(log n) call-stack space, while a bottom-up version can use O(1) auxiliary space because it does not need an array buffer. Quicksort can be implemented on a linked list, so I would not say it requires random access. It is simply a less natural fit: partitioning and reconnecting sub-lists is awkward, it loses the cache-friendly indexed partition available on arrays, and a poor pivot can still lead to O(n²). So the preference comes from predictable time and easy pointer-based merging, not from quicksort being impossible on a list.

questions.question: What is a stable sort and why does it matter?
questions.title: Stable Sort Definition Importance
questions.direct_answer: A **stable sort** preserves the **relative order of equal elements**. If two records compare equal on the sort key, a stable sort keeps them in their original order; an unstable sort may swap them. It matters for **multi-key sorting** (sort by one field, then another, without scrambling the first) and any time the original order carries meaning. Merge and insertion sort are stable; quick, heap, and selection are not.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can define stability precisely and give a real reason it matters (multi-key sorting)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing stability with correctness, or not knowing which common sorts are stable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give the multi-key example: stable sort lets you sort by secondary then primary key

sections.title: What Stability Means
sections.content:
A sort is **stable** if elements that compare **equal** on the sort key keep their **original relative order** after sorting. Suppose you sort people by age, and two people are both 30 - a stable sort leaves them in the same order they appeared in the input; an unstable sort might flip them.

Why care? **Multi-key sorting**. To sort employees by department, and within each department by name, you sort by the **secondary** key (name) first, then by the **primary** key (department) with a **stable** sort - the stability preserves the name order within each department. Stability also matters when the input order itself is meaningful (e.g. insertion time). **Merge** and **insertion** sort are stable; **quicksort, heap sort, selection sort** are not.

sections.content:

sections.title: Multi-Key Sort Needs Stability
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Stability == correctness**: both produce sorted output; stability only fixes the order of equal keys.
- **Wrong sort order for multi-key**: sort the **secondary** key first, then the primary stably.
- **Assuming quicksort is stable**: it isn't; use merge/TimSort when order of equals matters.
- **Primitives**: stability is irrelevant for primitives (equal values are identical).

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Stable** = equal elements keep their **original order**.
- Enables **multi-key sorting** (secondary first, then primary stably).
- **Stable**: merge, insertion, TimSort, counting.
- **Unstable**: quicksort, heap, selection.
- Irrelevant for **primitives**; use `thenComparing` for clean multi-key sorts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A sort is stable if elements that are equal on the sort key keep their original relative order after sorting. So if I'm sorting people by age and two people are both thirty, a stable sort guarantees they appear in the same order they were in the input, while an unstable sort is free to swap them. It's important to note this is not about correctness; both stable and unstable sorts produce fully sorted output. Stability only governs what happens to elements that tie on the key. The reason it matters in practice is multi-key sorting. Say I want to sort employees primarily by department and, within each department, by name. The clean way is to sort by the secondary key, name, first, and then do a stable sort by the primary key, department. Because the second sort is stable, it preserves the name ordering I established within each department, so I get the combined ordering I want. If that second sort were unstable, it would scramble the names within each department and ruin the effect. Stability also matters whenever the original input order itself carries meaning, like insertion or arrival time. As for which sorts are stable: merge sort and insertion sort are stable, and so is TimSort, which is what Java uses for objects, and counting sort. Quicksort, heap sort, and selection sort are not stable. One last point: for primitive values stability is irrelevant, because two equal integers are genuinely identical, there's nothing to preserve. In Java I'd usually express multi-key sorting in one stable step using Comparator dot comparing then thenComparing.

questions.question: When would you use counting sort instead of comparison-based sorts?
questions.title: When to Use Counting Sort
questions.direct_answer: Use counting sort when the values are integer keys drawn from a small, known range. It counts how often each key appears, then rebuilds the sorted result in **O(n + k)** time, where `k` is the size of the value range. It can beat comparison sorts when `k` is reasonably close to `n`, but its **O(k)** counting storage makes it a poor choice for a huge or sparse range.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know why counting sort can beat the comparison-sort lower bound and can recognise the range-size condition that makes it practical.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looking only at the number of items and forgetting that memory and running time also depend on the distance between the smallest and largest key.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the frequency array, the O(n + k) cost, the sparse-range boundary, and how cumulative counts make the algorithm stable.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Best for **integer keys** in a small, known range.
- Count each value, then turn the counts back into sorted output.
- Time is **O(n + k)**; extra counting space is **O(k)**.
- Use an offset for negative values; avoid a huge or sparse range.
- Prefix counts plus right-to-left placement make it **stable**.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Counting sort is a non-comparison sorting algorithm for integer keys in a small, known range. Instead of comparing two values, it uses each value as an index and counts how many times that value appears.

For example, 100,000 exam scores can only be from 0 to 100. Counting sort needs 101 counters: one pass records the frequencies, and a scan from 0 to 100 produces the sorted scores. The time is O(n + k), where n is the number of items and k is the size of the key range.

A frequency-only version is enough for plain integers. To sort records and keep equal-key records in their original order, cumulative counts give final positions and records are placed into an output array from right to left. Negative values also work by subtracting the minimum value before indexing the count array.

The key range is the deciding limit. A few numbers spread between 0 and one billion would require too much memory and too long a range scan. Counting sort is a strong choice for dense, bounded integer keys; a comparison-based library sort is safer for general values or a wide, unknown range.

sections.title: How Counting Becomes Sorting
sections.content:
Take the input `[4, 2, 2, 1, 3]`. Its values lie between 1 and 4, so a count array with four useful positions is enough.

1. **Count:** the frequencies for 1 through 4 become `[1, 2, 1, 1]`.
2. **Order:** visit the counters from the smallest value to the largest.
3. **Emit:** write one `1`, two `2`s, one `3`, and one `4`, giving `[1, 2, 2, 3, 4]`.

No pair of input values was compared. That is why the comparison-sort lower bound does not apply: counting sort uses extra knowledge about the keys. Its cost is `n` visits to count plus `k` visits to scan the range.

For records, cumulative counts answer a stronger question: **what is the final ending position of each key?** Placing records from right to left then preserves the order of records with the same key, which makes the sort stable.

sections.title: Choose by the Shape of the Keys
sections.content:
| Input | Better fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 100,000 exam scores from 0–100 | Counting sort | Only 101 counters; `k` is tiny |
| 500 ages from 0–120 | Counting sort | Small, meaningful integer range |
| 500 IDs from 1–1,000,000,000 | Comparison sort | The range is far too sparse |
| Names or arbitrary objects | Comparison sort | No small integer key to index directly |

sections.title: Java Frequency Version
The Boundary That Decides
sections.content: Counting sort does not automatically win just because it is written as **O(n + k)**. If `n = 1,000` and keys span 0 to 100, `k = 101` and the method is attractive. If the same 1,000 keys span 0 to one billion, the count array and range scan are impractical. The useful decision is therefore based on **range density**, memory limits, and whether a stable record sort is required—not on Big-O notation alone.

questions.question: How does merge sort work and why is it always O(n log n)?
questions.title: Merge Sort Algorithm Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Merge sort** is **divide-and-conquer**: split the array in half, recursively sort each half, then **merge** the two sorted halves into one. It's **O(n log n) in every case** - log n levels of splitting, O(n) work to merge each level - regardless of input order. The cost is **O(n) extra space** for the merge. It's also **stable**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain the divide-merge structure and why it's guaranteed O(n log n) (unlike quicksort)
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking merge sort is in-place, or not explaining the log n levels x O(n) merge = O(n log n)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Tie the guarantee to balanced halving (always log n levels) and note the O(n) space tradeoff

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Divide-and-conquer**: split, sort halves, **merge**.
- **O(n log n)** in **all** cases (balanced halving -> log n levels x O(n)).
- **O(n)** auxiliary space - **not** in-place.
- **Stable** (use `<=` when merging).
- Great for **linked lists** and **external/stable** sorting.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Merge sort is the classic divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm, and it has three phases. First, divide: I split the array into two halves. Second, conquer: I recursively sort each half. Third, combine: I merge the two sorted halves into a single sorted array, by repeatedly comparing the front elements of each half and taking the smaller one. The reason it's always O of n log n, in the best, average, and worst case, comes from two parts. The splitting always cuts the array in half, so the recursion has log n levels, that's how many times you can halve n down to one. Then, at each level, merging all the pieces back together touches every element exactly once, which is O of n work per level. Multiply the log n levels by the O of n merge work per level and you get O of n log n. The key point is that this halving doesn't depend on the data at all, unlike quicksort, where a bad pivot can produce unbalanced partitions and an O of n squared worst case. Merge sort has no such failure mode, which is why its bound is guaranteed. The tradeoff is space: the merge step needs a temporary buffer, so merge sort uses O of n auxiliary space and is not in place. It's also stable, as long as I use a less-than-or-equal comparison when merging, so equal elements keep their order. And because it only needs sequential access, it's an excellent choice for sorting linked lists and for external sorting of data that doesn't fit in memory. For example, `[5, 2, 4, 1]` splits into `[5, 2]` and `[4, 1]`. Those halves become `[2, 5]` and `[1, 4]`, and the final merge produces `[1, 2, 4, 5]`.

sections.title: Why every merge level costs n
sections.content:
Merge sort divides the array until each piece has one element, then merges neighboring sorted pieces. A merge compares the front values and copies the smaller one, so two sorted halves become one sorted range.

**Worked example: `[5, 2, 4, 1]`**

Split it into `[5, 2]` and `[4, 1]`, then into single values. Merge to get `[2, 5]` and `[1, 4]`. The final merge compares 2 with 1, then 2 with 4, then 5 with 4, producing `[1, 2, 4, 5]`.

The recursion tree has `log n` levels because every split halves the range. At any one level, the merge operations together read and write all `n` elements. Multiplying `n` work per level by `log n` levels gives O(n log n) in the best, average, and worst cases; input order does not remove the merge levels.

For arrays, the usual implementation needs an O(n) temporary buffer, and recursive calls use O(log n) stack depth. Taking from the left half when equal values are compared makes it stable. Merge sort is therefore attractive when stable, predictable time matters, but its extra array memory is a real trade-off.

sections.title: Merge Sort Recursion
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[array of n] --> B[split in half] B --> C[sort left half
recursively] B --> D[sort right half
recursively] C --> E[merge two
sorted halves] D --> E E --> Z[sorted array
O(n log n)] ```

sections.title: Merge Sort with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'In-place'**: merge sort needs **O(n)** auxiliary space for the merge buffer.
- **Not explaining the guarantee**: it's log n levels x O(n) merge = O(n log n), data-independent.
- **Using `<` in merge**: use `<=` to keep it **stable**.
- **Off-by-one in indices**: `mid = lo + (hi-lo)/2`, recurse `[lo,mid]` and `[mid+1,hi]`.

sections.title: Predictable time versus extra memory
sections.content: Merge sort guarantees O(n log n) and can be stable, regardless of the starting order. On arrays it normally allocates an O(n) merge buffer, while quicksort can work largely in place and often has better cache behavior but a theoretical O(n²) worst case. On linked lists, merge sort becomes especially natural because sorted halves can be joined by relinking nodes; recursive implementations still use O(log n) call-stack space.
